3D Scale Conversion Reference

Slicer percentages for converting miniatures between tabletop systems — Warhammer, D&D, Bolt Action, Star Wars Legion, and more. These are the numbers I use myself, based on a 175cm human baseline with eye-level measurement. I print on a Bambu Lab A1 Mini. Your mileage may vary.

Don't know your model's scale? Measure it and find out in 10 seconds first.

Last updated: August 10, 2026

Search conversions

No conversions found. Try "28mm" or "1:35".

Conversion Details

Full breakdowns for every pair

1:100 to 1:35

Bridging the gap between 15mm wargaming and large scale model kits.

1-100-to-1-35

Slicer setting

285.7%

The math

(50.0mm / 17.5mm) × 100 = 285.7%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level16.0mm Eye
  • Target eye level45.7mm Eye
  • Scale factor285.7%

When you need this

I grab this when bringing older or smaller 1:100 models into a modern 1:35 collection. This is a huge jump — more than double or less than half. I only reach for this one on purpose, for display pieces, never for mixed armies.

Source: 1:100

1:100 is a ratio scale I know well. My scale for big tank battles and regiment-level games where table space is the enemy. I mostly see it in: Flames of War, Team Yankee, 15mm wargaming.

Note: 1:100 minis land around 17.5mm total — taller than 15mm eye-level figures. I always confirm what the maker means.

Target: 1:35

1:35 shows up in: Tamiya, Trumpeter, MiniArt. A true ratio scale rather than a gaming label. When I build armor and dioramas, this is my lane.

Note: I've measured 1:35 minis from different makers a full ±2mm apart — trust the caliper, not the box.

Print notes

I set my slicer to 285.7% and lock uniform scaling. 1:35 vehicles come off my FDM printer beautifully at 0.2mm layers with a 0.4mm nozzle.

1:100 to 28mm

Those tiny Flames of War infantry scaled up to D&D or Bolt Action height.

1-100-to-28mm

Slicer setting

160.0%

The math

(28.0mm / 17.5mm) × 100 = 160.0%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level16.0mm Eye
  • Target eye level28.0mm Eye
  • Scale factor160.0%

When you need this

I grab this when bringing older or smaller 1:100 models into a modern 28mm collection. This is a big upscale. I wouldn't run these side by side unless you convert the whole unit or army — otherwise the models look like different species.

Source: 1:100

1:100 is a ratio scale I know well. My scale for big tank battles and regiment-level games where table space is the enemy. I mostly see it in: Flames of War, Team Yankee, 15mm wargaming.

Note: 1:100 minis land around 17.5mm total — taller than 15mm eye-level figures. I always confirm what the maker means.

Target: 28mm

28mm shows up in: Dungeons & Dragons, Pathfinder, Bolt Action infantry. The classic tabletop standard I learned on. It measures to the eyes (160cm on a 175cm human), not the top of the head, so there's always a little extra hidden under the hair and helmet.

Note: I've held older sculpts that were closer to 25mm true-scale. Check the sculptor's baseline before you scale, or you'll mix two generations of minis.

Print notes

I set my slicer to 160.0% and lock uniform scaling. On my FDM rig I rarely compensate for 28mm; a touch of over-extrusion usually cancels out any cooling shrinkage.

1:100 to 32mm

Scaling my 15mm FoW troops up to match a Warhammer 40k army.

1-100-to-32mm

Slicer setting

182.9%

The math

(32.0mm / 17.5mm) × 100 = 182.9%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level16.0mm Eye
  • Target eye level32.0mm Eye
  • Scale factor182.9%

When you need this

I grab this when bringing older or smaller 1:100 models into a modern 32mm collection. This is a big upscale. I wouldn't run these side by side unless you convert the whole unit or army — otherwise the models look like different species.

Source: 1:100

1:100 is a ratio scale I know well. My scale for big tank battles and regiment-level games where table space is the enemy. I mostly see it in: Flames of War, Team Yankee, 15mm wargaming.

Note: 1:100 minis land around 17.5mm total — taller than 15mm eye-level figures. I always confirm what the maker means.

Target: 32mm

32mm shows up in: Warhammer 40,000, Age of Sigmar, Malifaux. Games Workshop drifted from 28mm to 32mm between 2014 and 2015 for more facial detail and heroic proportions — a change I felt immediately when my old armies started looking small.

Note: I've been burned by third-party sculptors labeling 35mm models as '32mm heroic.' Check the eye-level measurement, not the total height.

Print notes

I set my slicer to 182.9% and lock uniform scaling. 32mm is forgiving on my FDM printer; layer lines vanish into the bigger surfaces.

Slicer setting

200.0%

The math

(35.0mm / 17.5mm) × 100 = 200.0%

Based on 175cm human baseline, eye-level measurement (160cm).

Scale baselines

  • Source eye level16.0mm Eye
  • Target eye level35.0mm Eye
  • Scale factor200.0%

When you need this

I grab this when bringing older or smaller 1:100 models into a modern 35mm collection. This is a big upscale. I wouldn't run these side by side unless you convert the whole unit or army — otherwise the models look like different species.

Source: 1:100

1:100 is a ratio scale I know well. My scale for big tank battles and regiment-level games where table space is the enemy. I mostly see it in: Flames of War, Team Yankee, 15mm wargaming.

Note: 1:100 minis land around 17.5mm total — taller than 15mm eye-level figures. I always confirm what the maker means.

Target: 35mm

35mm shows up in: Star Wars: Legion, Marvel: Crisis Protocol, Kingdom Death. My pick when I want more canvas for freehand detail without going full display-bust territory.

Note: 35mm gets marketed as 'true 35mm' (realistic) vs 'heroic 35mm' (exaggerated). I always check which one I'm mixing in.

Print notes

I set my slicer to 200.0% and lock uniform scaling. For 35mm faces on FDM I swap to a 0.2mm nozzle at 0.06mm layers — worth the extra print time.

When you need this

Target: 75mm

75mm shows up in: Display busts, Miniature painting competitions, Scale 75 display line. Not a wargaming scale at all — this is what I use for contest pieces and the display cabinet.

Note: 75mm sculpts often come with separate heads or arms so painters can reach everything — I plan my supports around that.

Print notes

I set my slicer to 428.6% and lock uniform scaling. 75mm on FDM needs a 0.2mm nozzle and slow speeds; I push layer height down to get a finish I'm happy to show off.

Source: 32mm

32mm is a gaming scale I know well. Games Workshop drifted from 28mm to 32mm between 2014 and 2015 for more facial detail and heroic proportions — a change I felt immediately when my old armies started looking small. I mostly see it in: Warhammer 40,000, Age of Sigmar, Malifaux.

Note: I've been burned by third-party sculptors labeling 35mm models as '32mm heroic.' Check the eye-level measurement, not the total height.

Target: 28mm

28mm shows up in: Dungeons & Dragons, Pathfinder, Bolt Action infantry. The classic tabletop standard I learned on. It measures to the eyes (160cm on a 175cm human), not the top of the head, so there's always a little extra hidden under the hair and helmet.

Note: I've held older sculpts that were closer to 25mm true-scale. Check the sculptor's baseline before you scale, or you'll mix two generations of minis.

Print notes

I set my slicer to 87.5% and lock uniform scaling. On my FDM rig I rarely compensate for 28mm; a touch of over-extrusion usually cancels out any cooling shrinkage.

How these numbers are calculated

By kitsorix, 3D printing hobbyist

I use a 175cm human baseline with eye-level at 160cm. This is what most of the fantasy and sci-fi miniature hobby uses. Historical kits sometimes measure to top of head, which is why the matrix includes both where it matters.

The math is simple division. I print the result on my Bambu Lab A1 Mini before I post it. FDM materials are dimensionally stable within 0.5%, so the percentage you see is the percentage you get. Your mileage will vary.

These values are what works for me and what the community reports back as functional. Your printer, filament, and settings may vary. Always print a test piece.

Technical guide

Why is miniature scale inconsistent?

Five things I learned after mixing up miniatures from six manufacturers and measuring them with calipers. The numbers on the box rarely match the model.

In this guide

  1. 1Why does a 28mm miniature measure 30-32mm?
  2. 2Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry?
  3. 3Why do miniature hands keep getting bigger?
  4. 4How much height does a miniature base add?
  5. 5How do I calculate scale conversions for 3D printing?

I have been burned by this enough times that I built a calculator. You buy a box labeled "28mm," paint them up, and they look like teenagers next to your existing squad. One company's 28mm is another's 30mm. The industry ruler is made of rubber.

This is not poor quality control. It is scale creep — a decades-long drift where miniatures slowly put on bulk. I have watched players tear their hair out trying to build a coherent army. The truth is that "scale" in wargaming is less a mathematical constant and more a stylistic suggestion. To build a uniform force, you need to look past the label and understand the math.

1

Why does a 28mm miniature measure 30-32mm?

The discrepancy starts with where the manufacturer places their ruler. Historically, a 175cm human mapped to a 1:60 ratio — the "1 inch = 5 feet" standard. Mathematically that is 30mm. So why call it 28mm?

The answer is the reference point. As Alkony notes, manufacturers rarely tell you where they stop measuring:

"A 28mm miniature means that the size of the miniature will be 28mm from the feet of the mini to the chosen reference point."

— Alkony

In most cases that reference point is eye level, not top of head. It is easier for a sculptor to find the eyes than the crown of a head hidden under a helmet. Add the forehead and headgear, and a "28mm" model is actually 30-32mm in practice.

You are often buying 32mm models that have been grandfathered into a 28mm label for historical reasons.

2

Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry than 1:56?

Bolt Action says the official vehicle scale is 1:56. On paper this is correct for 28mm. Walk into any tournament and you will see Tamiya 1:48 kits dominating the motor pool. This is not an accident.

Warlord Games has an internal inconsistency. Their metal miniatures are traditional 28mm (closer to 1:52 or 1:56), but their newer plastic sprues are actually 32mm. These plastics are taller and bulkier, so a true 1:56 tank looks like a toy next to them. The volumetric bulk of the infantry makes the vehicle look like the crew would not fit inside.

"I believe they fit with the oversized nature of Warlord's infantry better than the actual Warlord tanks themselves."

— Reddit, r/boltaction

There is also a fiscal reality: 1:48 Tamiya kits are widely available at hobby shops and often cost half the price of official wargaming-branded 1:56 kits.

For the technical hobbyist, 1:48 is a rare win-win: better visual proportions and lower cost. Use my 1:48 to 32mm conversion and see how it looks on your table.

3

Why do miniature hands keep getting bigger?

"Heroic Scale" is not a lack of anatomical skill. It is a functional design choice. From three feet away — the standard tabletop distance — a realistically proportioned 28mm head is roughly the size of a peppercorn.

"From a tabletop distance, a realistically scaled figure will have unintelligible hands and heads, and if they are scaled up to be readable, the feet look tiny."

— Zandoria Studios

Sculptors exaggerate heads, hands, and weapons to make models readable and easier to paint. This has led to what Warlord Games forums call the "Stay Puft Marshmallow Man" effect.

You can see this in the new plastic German Veteran and US Airborne kits. They are so puffy that they are incompatible with older true-scale kits. A new-style arm on an old-style body looks like a prosthetic from a different species.

Before you commit to a conversion, cross-reference the source scales in my conversion details below.

4

How much height does a miniature base add?

The most overlooked factor is not the model. It is the plastic disc it stands on. Infantry are almost always based on 2mm to 5mm thick plastic. Vehicles in historical games are often left unbased.

This creates a 3-5mm false height. A 32mm soldier on a 4mm base has his eye level at 36mm above the table. Next to a 1:56 Tiger tank resting directly on the mat, he towers over the engine deck.

This gap is why official scales feel wrong. The base raises the infantry's effective scale while the vehicle stays grounded.

3D printing is the equalizer. You no longer have to accept the manufacturer's fixed height. You can scale digitally to compensate for base thickness and ensure infantry and armor share the same visual horizon. My Scale Engine accounts for both eye level and top of head methodologies.

5

How do I calculate scale conversions for 3D printing?

Digital manufacturing shifts power from the factory to the player. Using a 175cm human baseline, I bridge the gap between 28mm (D&D/Historical) and 32mm (Warhammer/Modern) systems. When mixing STL files from different designers, you need to account for both measurement methodology and material physics.

What I do in practice

28mm true scale to 32mm heroic

I set my slicer to 114.3% for eye level, or <span class="text-white font-mono">116.1%</span> for top of head.

Material compensation

PLA and PETG shrink under 0.5% during cooling. I do not add compensation for FDM because the effect is smaller than normal print variation.

The number I actually use

To match a realistic 28mm soldier to a modern heroic system with material cooling accounted for, I land on 115.8%. Your printer may want something different.

You will find these in the conversion details above.

Scale conversion FAQ

What percentage do I scale 28mm to 32mm?
Type 114.3% into your slicer. That is the number for 28mm to 32mm measured to eye level. If you measure to the top of the head instead, use 116.1%. I have tested this on PLA with no additional shrinkage compensation needed.
How big is a 28mm miniature in real measurements?
A 28mm miniature represents a 175cm human at roughly 1:56 to 1:60 ratio scale. The miniature stands about 30-32mm to the top of the head, with the eye level at 28mm. Add 2-5mm for the base thickness and you have the total height sitting on your table.
What is the difference between 28mm and 32mm scale?
28mm is the classic tabletop standard — measured to eye level on a 175cm human with realistic proportions. 32mm heroic scale uses the same baseline but exaggerates heads, hands, and weapons so details read at arm's length. The height difference is only 14.3%, but the added bulk makes them feel a lot bigger on the table. Full conversion guide
What scale is 1:35 in mm for miniatures?
At 1:35, a 175cm human works out to about 50mm to the eyes. That is significantly bigger than 28mm tabletop miniatures — most 1:35 kits are Tamiya-style military models, not wargaming miniatures. If you want to mix a 1:35 tank with 28mm infantry, scale it down to 62.5% in your slicer.
Does PLA or PETG shrink after printing?
Barely. PLA and PETG can shrink 0.2% to 0.5% as they cool from printing temperature. This is small enough to ignore for miniature scaling. I do not add compensation for FDM because over-extrusion and cooling shrinkage tend to cancel each other out.
Why do 1:48 tanks look better with 28mm infantry than 1:56?
Here is the thing — most modern 28mm plastics from Warlord Games and similar manufacturers actually measure closer to 30-32mm. A true 1:56 tank looks undersized next to them. 1:48 Tamiya kits match the heroic proportions better, and they are often cheaper than official wargaming vehicles. I use 1:48 for my Bolt Action motor pool and nobody has complained at tournaments. Use my 1:48 to 28mm guide and see how it looks on your table.
What does "Eye Level" vs "Top of Head" mean in miniature scale?
Eye level means measuring from the foot to the centre of the eye — 160cm on a 175cm human. Top of head means measuring to the crown at 175cm. That 15cm gap creates a 5-10% difference in your scale calculations. Fantasy and sci-fi miniatures usually use eye level because helmets and top-knots vary. Historical kits tend to use top of head. The STL scale converter supports both.
How do I scale STL files for different tabletop games?
Find your source and target scales in the conversion details below, type the percentage into your slicer, and lock the XYZ axes to uniform scaling. Always print a test piece before committing to a full batch. The STL scale calculator on the homepage does this automatically — pick your scales, copy the number, done.
